questions.question: Benjamin Franklin led a royal commission that tested Franz Mesmer's 'animal magnetism' in 1784. Mesmer taught that an unseen fluid flowed from a healer into the sick and stirred up fits that cured them. The chemist Antoine Lavoisier planned two kinds of trial: in some, patients were magnetised without knowing it, and in others, patients were told they were being magnetised when they were not. What were the two kinds of trial built to tell apart?
questions.answer: The fluid and the patients' belief
choices: The fluid and the patients' belief
The fluid and an iron magnet's pull
The honest patients and the fakers
The fluid up close and from far away
questions.context: Lavoisier's plan pulled the two possible causes apart: if the fluid were real, patients magnetised in secret would react, and if belief were the cause, patients who only thought they were being treated would react. Blindfolds and screens kept the patients from knowing, which makes these trials among the first blind tests on record. The plan could not tell an honest patient from a faker, and Mesmer himself had long since given up iron magnets, saying the cure came from his fluid.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.M3) teaches how scientists test an explanation against evidence; the Franklin commission's two kinds of blind trial are a classic case of separating two possible causes.

questions.question: Charles d'Eslon, a doctor who followed Mesmer's method, let Benjamin Franklin's commission test his patients. The commissioners persuaded one woman, sitting blindfolded, that d'Eslon was magnetising her, though he was not in the room. Another woman was magnetised for half an hour from behind a paper screen, and no one said a word to her about it. Which of the two women fell into a fit during her trial?
questions.answer: Only the one who believed it
choices: Only the one who believed it
Only the one truly treated
Both of them, about equally
Neither of them at all
questions.context: The blindfolded woman fell into a fit within about three minutes though nothing at all was done to her, while the woman behind the screen showed nothing in half an hour of real magnetising. Belief alone brought on a real fit. An effect like this, caused by expecting a treatment rather than by the treatment itself, is now called a placebo effect.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M3) teaches that a test must rule out the subject's own expectation; the placebo effect, belief alone producing a felt effect, is the plain-words idea behind blinding.

questions.question: Charles d'Eslon magnetised one apricot tree in Benjamin Franklin's garden at Passy and brought a boy he had found sensitive to Mesmer's fluid. The boy was blindfolded and led from tree to tree, hugging each for two minutes, and he fell into a fit at the fourth, a tree that d'Eslon had never touched. What did the commission conclude had brought on fits like his?
choices: The patients' own imagination
Fluid that spread from tree to tree
A fluid too faint to be measured
Tricks the healers had taught them
questions.context: The commissioners reported that nothing proved the fluid existed, and they put the fits down to imagination, helped along by touch and by patients imitating one another. The fits were real enough; what brought them on was belief, not a fluid, and a fluid that no one could detect explained nothing. The report was printed in at least 20,000 copies and spread across France and beyond.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M3) teaches that science explains what happens in nature from evidence; the commission's verdict, imagination and not an unseen fluid, is a classic claim settled by blind tests.

questions.question: Thirteen judges, among them a vet, a circus manager, a cavalry officer, several schoolteachers and the director of the Berlin zoo, watched Wilhelm von Osten's horse, Clever Hans, answer questions by tapping a hoof. In September 1904 they reported that no tricks were involved. Oskar Pfungst, an assistant to the panel's leader, Carl Stumpf, went on testing the horse. What did his tests show about the judges' report?
questions.answer: No one cheated, yet Hans was not counting
choices: No one cheated, yet Hans was not counting
No one cheated, and Hans really was counting
Von Osten cheated, giving Hans secret signs
A helper cheated, signalling from the crowd
questions.context: The judges were right that no one was cheating: von Osten believed in his horse and charged nothing to watch him, and Hans did as well for strangers as for his owner. But ruling out tricks did not show that Hans could count, and Pfungst found that the answers came from the questioners, not from the horse. Finding no tricks had left the real question open.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M3) teaches that findings vary in certainty and are revised in light of new evidence; the 1904 panel's verdict, right about fraud but not the whole story, is the case.

questions.question: Wilhelm von Osten, a retired mathematics teacher in Berlin, believed that his horse, Clever Hans, could do sums, spell and tell the time, answering by tapping a hoof. Oskar Pfungst set out to learn how Hans did it, and he changed the tests one way after another to see which change made the horse fail. Which change was it?
questions.answer: A questioner who did not know the answer
choices: A questioner who did not know the answer
A questioner Hans had never met before
A question written down, not spoken aloud
A test with his owner out of the room
questions.context: Hans did as well for strangers, for written questions and with von Osten away, so no one was feeding him answers on purpose. He failed only when the questioner did not know the answer himself, or stood where Hans could not see him: the answers had been coming from the questioner all along.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M3) teaches that scientists test an explanation by changing conditions and examining the results that do not fit; Pfungst's questioner who did not know the answer is the classic blind test.

questions.question: Oskar Pfungst fitted Clever Hans with blinders, shields beside the eyes that block a horse's side view, so that a questioner could stand either in the horse's sight or just out of it. With the questioner in sight, Hans answered 50 of 56 questions rightly. How many of 35 did he answer rightly with the questioner out of his sight?
choices: 2 of the 35
16 of the 35
24 of the 35
31 of the 35
questions.context: Hans got about 89 percent right while he could see the person asking, and about 6 percent once he could not. He wore the blinders in both kinds of trial, so the blinders were not what made him fail; what changed was whether he could watch the questioner. His answers came from watching, not from counting.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M1) teaches reading what data show; the drop from 50 of 56 to 2 of 35 when Hans could not see the questioner is the key result of the Clever Hans tests.

questions.question: Oskar Pfungst watched Clever Hans's questioners closely as the horse tapped out answers with a hoof. Each questioner watched the hoof closely and waited, tense, as the taps went on. Pfungst found that something the questioner did at the right count told Hans to stop. What was it?
questions.answer: A tiny upward jerk of the head
choices: A tiny upward jerk of the head
A soft click made with the tongue
A small tap of a foot on the ground
A quiet word said under the breath
questions.context: When the count reached the right number, the questioner's tension eased and his head rose a very little, about a millimetre by one account, and Hans stopped on that movement. No questioner knew he was making it, which is why the 1904 panel, looking for tricks, found none.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M3) teaches that scientists examine results closely instead of ignoring what does not fit; the questioner's unnoticed head movement was the mechanism Pfungst found.

questions.question: Oskar Pfungst learned exactly which tiny movement Clever Hans was reading, the sign that told the horse to stop tapping. Then Pfungst stood before Hans and asked the questions himself, knowing the cue well. What happened?
questions.answer: He gave Hans the cue without meaning to
choices: He gave Hans the cue without meaning to
He held still, so Hans could not answer
He held still, yet Hans answered anyway
He found Hans read only von Osten's cues
questions.context: Pfungst found himself giving the same tiny signs without meaning to, as von Osten and the strangers had. A questioner cannot simply decide not to give a cue, so a fair test keeps the answer from the questioner, or keeps the questioner out of sight. The trap is now called the Clever Hans effect, and experiments are still built to avoid it.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M3) teaches that scientific knowledge is limited by human capacity; an honest tester's unnoticed cues are such a limit, and keeping the tester blind is the fix.

questions.question: Emily Rosa was nine when she first tested therapeutic touch practitioners in 1996, for a school science fair. Each practitioner put both hands through holes at the foot of a tall screen. Emily held her own hand above one of them, picked by a coin toss, and the practitioner had to say which, by sensing what practitioners call the human energy field. Over 280 trials in 1996 and 1997, 21 practitioners named the right hand 123 times. What does that score show?
questions.answer: No sense of her field, only guessing
choices: No sense of her field, only guessing
A weak sense, right almost half the time
A true sense, but read the wrong way round
A true sense, dulled by the screen between them
questions.context: With two hands to choose from, pure guessing names the right one about half the time, or about 140 times in 280. The practitioners' 123, or 44 percent, is within the range that guessing gives, so the test found no sign that they could feel her hand; a score a little under half is chance at work, not a sense working backward. The study's authors noted that a true ability should have found her hand every time.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M1) teaches what data can and cannot show; comparing a score with what chance alone gives (half right, with two choices) is that skill.

questions.question: Before Emily Rosa's trials began, the authors of her study decided that a practitioner would pass by naming the right hand at least 8 times in 10, while guessing would give about 5. Scientists who test a claim often fix what will count as success ahead of time, like this. Why fix it ahead of time?
questions.answer: So the mark cannot shift after the results
choices: So the mark cannot shift after the results
So luck alone can never earn anyone a pass
So the people tested have no way to cheat
So the trials can stop as soon as one passes
questions.context: A pass mark fixed beforehand is a line drawn before anyone has seen a score, so a poor result cannot be excused by lowering it, nor an ordinary one dressed up as a success. It does not stop luck: guessing alone reaches 8 of 10 about once in 18 tries, which is why the mark sat well above the 5 that guessing gives. Many scientists now post such plans publicly before they gather any data.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.M3) teaches that science judges explanations by evidence; deciding before a test what result counts as success keeps that judgement honest.
